analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose pay terms, give paystubs, and repay stolen wages with multiplied damages.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Labor Committee approved it 27-19, but the bill never reached the House floor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amended federal wage law to make it easier for workers to get paid what they are owed. It would have required employers to give workers written terms of employment and itemized paystubs, pay final wages within two weeks of a job ending, and honor contract wage rates. It raised the penalties for shorting workers — double or triple damages, larger per-employee fines, and mandatory referral of willful violators to the Justice Department for prosecution — and voided arbitration clauses that force workers out of court on wage claims. It also created a $50 million-a-year grant program to help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers who are shorted on pay: restaurant, retail, building services, home care, warehouse, and agricultural workers, plus workers whose union contracts promise wages above the legal minimum. Nonprofit legal aid and worker-advocacy groups would have gained grant funding to help them file claims.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to give new hires a written statement of their pay rate, how they are paid, and whether they are classified as exempt from minimum wage and overtime rules, in the worker's primary language, plus updated statements when terms change.
Every pay period would come with an itemized paystub showing hours worked, rates, gross and net pay, overtime hours, and each deduction.
Final pay for all hours worked would be due within 14 days of a job ending; an employer who is late owes the worker their regular pay for each day of delay, up to 30 days.
Employers would have to pay the wage rate promised in a contract or union agreement even when it exceeds the federal minimum, and all such unpaid wages would be recoverable in court.

Workers who win wage claims would collect interest plus double the unpaid wages in liquidated damages, triple for willful violations; civil fines would rise to as much as $22,030 per affected employee, and $110,150 for repeat or willful violations.

Employers who willfully short workers, falsify wage records, or retaliate would have to be referred by the Labor Department to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution, with criminal fines of $10,000 per affected employee.

Workers could not be forced to sign away their right to go to court over wages as a condition of employment; pre-dispute arbitration agreements could not block a wage claim, including class and collective claims.
The window to sue over unpaid wages would stretch from 2 years to 4 (3 to 5 for willful violations), and the clock would pause while the Labor Department investigates an employer.

Workers could get copies of their own wage records within 21 days, and if an employer's records are incomplete, the worker's own credible testimony would create a presumption that their account of hours and wages is accurate.

The Labor Department could award $50 million a year through fiscal 2026 to nonprofits, labor organizations, legal aid groups, and others to educate workers, help them file claims, and train employers on compliance.

Willful wage violators would face mandatory referral to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution, and civil fines would rise to $22,030 per affected employee and $110,150 for repeat or willful violations.
The window to sue over unpaid wages would stretch from 2 years to 4, and from 3 to 5 years for willful violations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with wage-and-hour violations, who would owe multiplied back pay, interest, and larger fines, and could face criminal referral for willful violations. Compliant employers — especially small and multi-state businesses — would bear new paperwork costs for disclosures and paystubs and longer legal exposure for past pay practices.

drawbacks.text: The disclosure, paystub, and recordkeeping requirements impose real compliance costs, especially on small employers and those operating in multiple states, though the bill directs the Labor Department to provide model forms and compliance assistance.

Double and triple damages on top of a 4-to-5-year lookback and a presumption favoring the worker when records are incomplete would raise litigation exposure even for employers making good-faith mistakes.
Enforcing every promised contract wage rate — not just the legal minimum — extends federal enforcement into private agreements that parties negotiated themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The enforcement teeth are the point: millions of workers are shorted on wages each year and the current system makes recovery slow and rarely worth the effort. The compliance burden on honest employers is real but modest — model forms and assistance are provided — and the heaviest costs (multiplied damages, larger fines, criminal referral) fall on violations, willful ones especially. The arbitration and statute-of-limitations changes are the most contested, since they expand employer legal exposure well beyond current practice.

outcome.mechanism: The Labor Committee approved it 27-19 and printed it on the House calendar, but no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 10, 2022, by Rep. Rosa DeLauro and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On May 18, 2022, the committee met, marked the bill up, and ordered it reported as amended by a vote of 27-19.
On October 7, 2022, the committee formally reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 117-540) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the House's list of bills awaiting floor consideration.
The bill never received a House floor vote and saw no Senate action; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired.
All 45 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers, since the paystub rules, multiplied damages, longer deadlines, and criminal referrals never took effect, and members avoided a recorded floor vote on the measure.

against.name: Rep. Nancy Pelosi

sides.party_line_note: All 45 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the committee vote of 27-19 left 19 members opposed.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, building services, home care, agriculture)
industries.note: These industries have high rates of wage-and-hour violations; the bill would have imposed paystub and disclosure requirements, double or triple damages, per-employee fines of up to $110,150, and criminal referral for willful violations. The bill died, so none of this took effect.
The bill would have voided pre-dispute arbitration clauses for wage claims, restoring workers' access to court, including class and collective actions.

industries.industry: Nonprofit worker-advocacy and legal aid organizations
industries.note: Eligible for the bill's $50 million-a-year grant program to educate workers about their rights, help them file claims, and train employers on compliance.
